messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Input: Piezoelectric energy harvester (Ip, f, Cp, RL).
    *   Goal: Provide power to RL at node "out".
    *   Constraints:
        *   $v_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $v_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$ (S1-S6)
    *   Piezo source: $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25-30nF) and $R_{leak}$ (20M$\Omega$).
    *   Open-circuit voltage: $V_{oc} = I_p / (2\pi f C_p) \approx 3.2\text{V}$.

    *   S1 (Nominal): ok except settled (dv).
    *   S2 (Heavy load): $v_{avg}$ too low (1.76V), $t_{up}$ too slow.
    *   S3 (Strong excitation, light load): $v_{max}$ too high (5.72V), $v_{pp}$ too high, settled fail.
    *   S4 (Weak excitation): $v_{avg}$ too low (1.51V), $t_{up}$ too slow.
    *   S5 (Low frequency): settled fail.
    *   S6 (Hot, Cp+20%): all ok.

    *   *Voltage Low (S2, S4):* Need a more efficient conversion than a simple bridge. The open-circuit voltage (3.2V) is quite low given diode drops ($\sim 0.25\text{V} \times 2$ for bridge = $0.5\text{V}$). An active rectifier or an SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) circuit can increase the extracted energy.
    *   *Voltage Too High (S3):* Need a voltage clamp. A Zener diode (DZ33) on the output capacitor is the standard way to prevent overvoltage.
    *   *Ripple ($v_{pp}$):* Large output capacitor (Cout) helps.
    *   *Startup ($t_{up}$):* More efficient harvesting (like SSHI) reduces startup time.
    *   *Settled ($dv$):* Large Cout helps stabilize the mean voltage.

    *   **Topology 1: Full Bridge Rectifier (FBR) + Zener Clamp.**
        *   Basic FBR but with a DZ33 to prevent $v_{max} > 3.6\text{V}$.
        *   This solves S3's overvoltage but might still fail S2/S4's undervoltage.

    *   **Topology 2: SSHI-like (Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor).**
        *   SSHI uses an inductor and a switch to "flip" the voltage on $C_p$ at the peaks, significantly increasing the energy extracted.
        *   Basic SSHI (Parallel-SSHI):
            *   $L$ in series with a switch $S$.
            *   Switch $S$ closes at the voltage extrema of $C_p$.
            *   Wait, the simplified SSHI circuit often looks like: Piezo $\rightarrow$ Bridge $\rightarrow$ Cout, with an inverter $L+S$ across the piezo.
            *   Alternative: A synchronous rectifier (using SYNC and switches) instead of diodes.

    *   **Topology 3: Synchronous Rectifier (Active Bridge).**
        *   Using switches instead of diodes reduces the voltage drop (DSCH is $0.25\text{V}$, Ron is $2\Omega$).
        *   With $I_p \approx 50\mu\text{A}$, $I \cdot R_{on}$ is negligible ($\approx 100\mu\text{V}$), compared to $0.25\text{V}$.
        *   This helps S2 and S4 significantly.

    *   S3 ($v_{max}$ failure) is the most restrictive for the upper bound.
    *   S2/S4 ($v_{avg}$ failure) are the most restrictive for the lower bound.
    *   The reference design (FBR) is close but fails S2, S4 on voltage and S3 on overvoltage.

    *   *Proposal A: FBR + Zener.* (Simple fix for S3).
    *   *Proposal B: Parallel SSHI.* (Inductor-Switch flip to boost energy for S2/S4, plus Zener for S3).
    *   *Proposal C: Synchronous Rectifier.* (Replace diodes with SYNC-controlled switches to reduce drop for S2/S4, plus Zener for S3).

    Wait, let's refine the SSHI. A basic "Parallel-SSHI" (or P-SSHI) uses an inductor and a switch to invert the charge on the piezo capacitor.
    The circuit:
    - Piezo (pzp, pzn)
    - Diode bridge from (pzp, pzn) to (out, 0)
    - L and S across the piezo? Or $L$ and $S$ connected in a specific way?
    Actually, the prompt suggests $L-C_p$ inversion. A simple one:
    - $L$ between pzp and a node `n1`.
    - $S$ between `n1` and pzn.
    - SYNC `G1` controls $S$ at `edges: both`, `ton` $\approx \pi\sqrt{L C_p}$.
    - This inverts the voltage on $C_p$ at the peaks, increasing the voltage that reaches the bridge.

    Let's refine Proposal B:
    - Rectifier: Full Bridge (DSCH) from (pzp, pzn) to (out, 0).
    - Inverter: L1(pzp, n1), S1(n1, pzn), G1(SYNC) controls S1.
    - Protection: D_zener(0, out) model DZ33.
    - Storage: C_out(out, 0).

    Wait, the reference design is:
    - FBR (4x DSCH)
    - C_out (2.2uF)
    - Result: S2 $v_{avg} = 1.76\text{V}$, S4 $v_{avg} = 1.51\text{V}$.
    - We need to push these above 1.8V.
    - FBR drop is $\sim 0.5\text{V}$. If we use a synchronous rectifier, we save $\sim 0.5\text{V}$.
    - For S4, $1.51\text{V} + 0.5\text{V} = 2.01\text{V}$, which is $> 1.8\text{V}$.

    Let's design the Synchronous Rectifier (Active Bridge):
    - S1(pzp, out), S2(pzn, out), S3(0, pzp), S4(0, pzn).
    - This requires 4 switches and 2 SYNCs (one for positive half, one for negative).
    - Or use a bridge of diodes and a boost? No, too many components.
    - Let's stick to:
        1. FBR + Zener (Check if Zener alone fixes S3).
        2. SSHI (FBR + L-S inverter + Zener).
        3. Synchronous Rectifier (Active bridge + Zener).

    Wait, 16 component limit.
    Active Bridge:
    - 4 switches
    - 2 SYNCs
    - 1 Zener
    - 1 Cout
    - Total: 8 components. This is very efficient.

    Let's detail the active bridge:
    - G1 (edges: pos): S1(pzp, out), S2(0, pzn)
    - G2 (edges: neg): S3(pzn, out), S4(0, pzp)
    - G1 activates at the piezo positive peak? No, SYNC "closes its switches for ton seconds at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero crossings of the piezo current."
    - Piezo current $I = I_p \sin(\omega t)$.
    - Zero crossings of $I$ are at $t = 0, T/2, T, \dots$
    - These are the voltage extrema of $C_p$ (since $V = \int I/C dt$).
    - At $t=0$ (positive peak of $V$), we want to connect pzp to out and pzn to 0.
    - At $t=T/2$ (negative peak of $V$), we want to connect pzn to out and pzp to 0.
    - SYNC `edges: pos` likely triggers at the positive peak. `edges: neg` at the negative peak.
    - Wait, the prompt says "closes its switches for ton seconds... at the piezo voltage extrema".
    - If `edges: both`, it triggers at both.
    - For an active bridge:
        - At $V_{max}$ (positive peak): pzp $\rightarrow$ out, pzn $\rightarrow$ 0. (Switch S1, S2)
        - At $V_{min}$ (negative peak): pzn $\rightarrow$ out, pzp $\rightarrow$ 0. (Switch S3, S4)

    Actually, a simpler active bridge is:
    - SYNC G1 (edges: both) controls:
        - S1(pzp, out) and S2(0, pzn) when positive peak? No, SYNC only controls switches. It doesn't have "if positive" logic for the *same* SYNC.
        - Wait, "edges: pos" and "edges: neg" are available!
        - G1 (edges: pos): S1(pzp, out), S2(0, pzn)
        - G2 (edges: neg): S3(pzn, out), S4(0, pzp)

    But wait, is a synchronous rectifier better than a diode bridge?
    A diode bridge is *always* conducting when the voltage is higher than the threshold.
    A synchronous rectifier only conducts for `ton` seconds.
    If `ton` is too short, we lose energy.
    If `ton` is too long, we short the capacitor.
    Diode bridges are generally more robust for energy harvesting unless the $V_{oc}$ is very low.
    Here $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{V}$. The diode drop is $0.5\text{V}$.
    Maybe the SSHI (inductor flip) is more powerful.

    SSHI Rationale:
    The L-S inverter flips the charge on $C_p$. Instead of $C_p$ charging from 0 to $V_{oc}$, it effectively sees a much higher voltage, pushing more charge through the rectifier. This is a well-known technique for piezos.

    - FBR: 4x DSCH
    - Inverter: L1, S1, G1 (SYNC)
    - Clamp: DZ33
    - Storage: C_out
    - Total components: 4 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 9 components.

    Connectivity:
    - D1: pzp $\rightarrow$ out
    - D2: pzn $\rightarrow$ out
    - D3: 0 $\rightarrow$ pzp
    - D4: 0 $\rightarrow$ pzn
    - L1: pzp $\rightarrow$ n1
    - S1: n1 $\rightarrow$ pzn (Ctrl: G1)
    - G1: SYNC (edges: both, ton: $\sim \pi\sqrt{LC_p}$)
    - DZ1: 0 $\rightarrow$ out (Cathode on out)
    - C1: out $\rightarrow$ 0

    Wait, is the L-S inverter correct?
    In P-SSHI, the inductor and switch are in parallel with the piezo.
    Piezo is between pzp and pzn.
    So L1 and S1 should be in parallel with (pzp, pzn).
    L1: pzp $\rightarrow$ n1
    S1: n1 $\rightarrow$ pzn
    This is exactly what I wrote.

    Wait, the reference FBR used $C_{out} = 2.2\mu\text{F}$. Let's use a similar value.
    For $L$, $\pi\sqrt{L C_p} \approx 10-50\mu\text{s}$.
    If $C_p = 25\text{nF}$, $L = 10\text{mH} \implies \pi\sqrt{10^{-2} \cdot 25 \cdot 10^{-9}} = \pi \cdot 5 \cdot 10^{-6} \approx 15\mu\text{s}$.

    Let's consider one more: A simple FBR + Zener. If $V_{oc} = 3.2\text{V}$ and $V_{out} = 1.8\text{V}$, the bridge should work for S1, S5, S6. S2 and S4 are the problem. FBR is failing S2/S4. The active rectifier or SSHI is needed.

    Let's refine the three proposals:
    1. **FBR_Zener**: FBR + DZ33 + C_out. (Baseline improvement for S3).
    2. **SSHI_Zener**: FBR + L-S Inverter + DZ33 + C_out. (Boosts $v_{avg}$, fixes S2/S4, fixes S3).
    3. **SyncRect_Zener**: Active Bridge (4 switches, 2 SYNCs) + DZ33 + C_out. (Reduces voltage drop, fixes S2/S4, fixes S3).

    *Self-Correction on SyncRect:*
    If I use 4 switches:
    S1(pzp, out), S2(0, pzn) controlled by G1 (edges: pos)
    S3(pzn, out), S4(0, pzp) controlled by G2 (edges: neg)
    Wait, the "extrema" occur at zero-crossings of the current.
    Positive current peak $\rightarrow$ $V$ is crossing zero.
    Current zero-crossing $\rightarrow$ $V$ is at peak.
    So at $t=0$, $I=0$ and $V$ is at a peak.
    If $V$ is positive peak, we want pzp $\rightarrow$ out and pzn $\rightarrow$ 0.
    If $V$ is negative peak, we want pzn $\rightarrow$ out and pzp $\rightarrow$ 0.
    This matches the SyncRect design.

    *Refining the SSHI Inverter:*
    The inductor $L$ and switch $S$ are in parallel with $C_p$.
    When $S$ closes, $L$ and $C_p$ form a resonant circuit.
    The charge on $C_p$ is transferred to $L$ and then back to $C_p$ with opposite polarity.
    $V_{C_p}$ goes from $+V_{peak}$ to $-V_{peak}$ (approximately).
    This "flips" the voltage, effectively doubling the voltage swing and allowing more charge to be pushed through the rectifier.

    Let's check component counts again.
    SyncRect: 4 S, 2 SYNC, 1 DZ33, 1 C = 8 components.
    SSHI: 4 D, 1 L, 1 S, 1 SYNC, 1 DZ33, 1 C = 9 components.

    One detail: `ton` for SSHI.
    $\pi\sqrt{L C_p}$ is the half-period of the resonant $LC$ circuit.
    For $L=10\text{mH}, C=25\text{nF}$, $T_{res} = 2\pi\sqrt{LC} \approx 31.4\mu\text{s}$.
    So $t_{on} = T_{res}/2 \approx 15.7\mu\text{s}$.
    The evolution strategy will optimize this.

    Let's double check the bridge diodes' models. DSCH is low-drop.
    S3 is the one that goes too high (5.72V). DZ33 will clamp it to 3.3V.
    S2/S4 are the ones that go too low. SSHI or SyncRect will help.

    Final check on connectivity:
    FBR:
    D1: [pzp, out], D2: [pzn, out], D3: [0, pzp], D4: [0, pzn]
    - D1: pzp(+) $\rightarrow$ out(+) [OK]
    - D2: pzn(+) $\rightarrow$ out(+) [OK]
    - D3: 0 $\rightarrow$ pzp [Wait, anode 0, cathode pzp. If pzp is negative, it conducts. OK]
    - D4: 0 $\rightarrow$ pzn [Wait, anode 0, cathode pzn. If pzn is negative, it conducts. OK]
    This is a standard full bridge.

    SSHI inverter:
    L1: [pzp, n1], S1: [n1, pzn]
    - Parallel to piezo. OK.

    SyncRect:
    S1: [pzp, out], S2: [0, pzn], G1: pos
    S3: [pzn, out], S4: [0, pzp], G2: neg
    - When G1 is on, pzp $\rightarrow$ out and pzn $\rightarrow$ 0.
    - When G2 is on, pzn $\rightarrow$ out and pzp $\rightarrow$ 0.
    - This is a synchronous rectifier.

    Wait, a synchronous rectifier *only* conducts during `ton`. A diode bridge conducts for the *entire half-cycle* (whenever $V > V_{drop}$).
    A synchronous rectifier is only useful if `ton` is long enough or if it's used as a switch in a converter.
    For simple rectification, it's actually *less* efficient than diodes unless you have a very complex controller.
    SSHI is much more likely to work.

    Wait, maybe a simpler "half-wave" active rectifier? No, FBR is better.
    Let's stick with:
    1. FBR + DZ33 (The baseline "safe" move)
    2. SSHI + DZ33 (The "power" move)
    3. A variant of SSHI? Or maybe a Capacitor-multiplier? No, let's try a "Charge Pump" style or just keep the SyncRect as a possibility.
    Actually, a better third option would be a "Synchronous Rectifier" that acts like a diode. But we only have SYNC.
    Let's try "Half-bridge SSHI" or just a larger $C_{out}$ for the first one.
    Actually, the most robust options for piezo are SSHI and FBR.
    Let's try:
    1. FBR + DZ33
    2. SSHI (FBR + L-S) + DZ33
    3. SSHI with a different inverter (e.g., L and S on the output side? No, that's not how it works).

    Let's refine the SSHI one more time.
    In some SSHI versions, the switch and inductor are used to flip the voltage *before* the rectifier.
    This is called "Parallel SSHI".
    Piezo (pzp, pzn) || [L1 + S1].
    This is exactly what I have.

    What about the "Synchronous Rectifier" again? If I set `ton` to be very large (e.g., $0.001\text{s}$), it's almost like a diode (since the frequency is 100Hz, the half-period is $0.005\text{s}$). But `ton` max is $0.001\text{s}$.
    So for a 100Hz signal, `ton = 0.001` is only 20% of the half-cycle.
    This means we lose 80% of the energy.
    Synchronous rectification is not the way here.

    Let's use:
    1. `fbr_zener`: Basic FBR + Zener clamp.
    2. `sshi_zener`: Parallel SSHI + Zener clamp.
    3. `sshi_zener_large_c`: Same as sshi_zener but starting with a larger $C_{out}$ (though the optimizer handles $C_{out}$). Wait, the prompt says "different connectivity".

    Another topology: "Half-Bridge" rectifier? No, that's worse.
    How about a "Voltage Doubler" (Greinacher circuit)?
    - C1 (pzp to 0)
    - D1 (pzp to n1)
    - C2 (n1 to 0)
    - D2 (n1 to out)
    This doubles the voltage. $V_{oc}$ is 3.2V, so $V_{out}$ could be $\sim 6\text{V}$.
    With a Zener clamp at 3.3V, this could be very efficient for low-excitation cases (S2, S4).

    Let's compare:
    - FBR: $V_{out} \approx V_{oc} - 0.5\text{V} = 2.7\text{V}$
    - Doubler: $V_{out} \approx 2 \cdot V_{oc} - 1.0\text{V} = 5.4\text{V}$ (clamped to 3.3V)
    - SSHI: $V_{out}$ is boosted by flipping $C_p$ charge.

    Let's go with:
    1. `fbr_zener`
    2. `sshi_zener`
    3. `doubler_zener`

    Refining `doubler_zener`:
    - D1: [pzp, n1]
    - C1: [pzp, 0]
    - D2: [n1, out]
    - C2: [n1, 0]
    - DZ1: [0, out]
    - C_out: [out, 0]
    This only uses the positive half-cycle. Let's make it a full-wave doubler.
    - Bridge to (n1, 0)
    - C_pump: [n1, 0]
    - D_out: [n1, out]
    - C_out: [out, 0]
    - DZ1: [0, out]
    This is essentially a rectifier followed by a charge pump.

    Let's simplify:
    Proposal 1: FBR + Zener (Baseline)
    Proposal 2: SSHI + Zener (Advanced)
    Proposal 3: Voltage Doubler + Zener (Alternative boost)

    Wait, the "doubler" can be simply:
    - FBR (pzp, pzn) $\rightarrow$ (n1, 0)
    - C_pump: [n1, 0]
    - D_out: [n1, out] (But we need to shift it... this is not a doubler).
    A real doubler:
    - D1: [pzp, n1], C1: [pzp, 0]
    - D2: [n1, out], C2: [n1, 0]
    (And a similar set for pzn). This is getting complex.

    Let's stick to the most promising:
    1. `fbr_zener`
    2. `sshi_zener`
    3. `sshi_zener_extra` (maybe a different inverter config? No).

    Actually, let's try the Synchronous Rectifier one more time, but instead of `ton` being small, what if we use the SYNC to *flip* the polarity of the piezo?
    Wait, the SSHI *is* that.
